newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers talks deadlocked, strikes tighten.
newsitem.headline: French truckers talks deadlocked, strikes tighten.

text.p: Marathon talks between striking French truck drivers and employers broke off in deadlock on Monday as protesters tightened their grip with barricades extending to Channel ports and the German border.

Overnight talks between the two sides with a state mediator ended with no breakthroughs after almost 14 hours at the French Transport Ministry in Paris over the strikes and blockades in their eighth day on Monday.
"That was 14 hours for nothing," said Roger Poletti, a leader of the Force Ouvriere union.

Both sides agreed to meet for more talks, hosted by government mediator Robert Cros, at 5 p.m. (1600 GMT) on Monday in a bid to resolve the truckers' demands for shorter working hours, wage rises and retirement at 55 instead of 60.

The truckers reinforced their actions on Monday, with barricades at five frontier posts with Germany and blockades for trucks at the northern ports of Calais and Boulogne, the major routes for ferries to Britain.

Cars and buses were allowed to embark on the ferries. The action added to the woes of cross-Channel travellers, already hit by the closure of the Channel Tunnel to all but freight trains after a fire last week.

The state road information centre said there were 98 truckers' barricades on major routes in France on Monday morning, against 62 on Sunday night. The figures do not count disruption to smaller routes.

The truckers also blocked fuel depots and roads around the nation in the toughest wave of unrest in France since a 24-day round of public sector strikes against the centre-right government almost paralysed the country in late 1995.

In the south-western city of Bordeaux, for instance, most petrol stations had run out of supplies. Bordeaux has been singled out for one of the tightest nooses because conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe is mayor of the city.
In the Paris area, access roads to the Rungis wholesale food market were blocked and the main autoroute north of the capital was cut to one lane on the southbound carriage around Roissy airport.
An IPSOS opinion poll for France-2 television showed 74 percent of French people sympathised with the strikers. It also revealed that 87 percent found their demands "rather justified".
Poletti called on strikers to tighten their action but stopped short of echoing some unionists' calls for strikes to spread to other sectors.

"I fear that almost all the big cities of France will be affected," Poletti said. But he said emergency supplies of fuel were assured and did not believe the government would order in troops to clear roads.
Truckers complain that they work long hours for low pay and say haulage companies do not usually pay them for waiting for loading and unloading in foreign warehouses.
